messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir was twenty years old when the assault happened, a night that had started with the familiar scent of jasmine perfume and ended with him walking home in the dark, unable to make sense of what had just occurred. He had been seeing a woman from his university for several months, someone he trusted, and when she invited him to her apartment that evening, he had no reason to suspect what would follow. The smell of jasmine became the central thread of that memory—it was on her skin, in the sheets, and it lingered in his hair and clothes long after. But it was not just the smell. What happened that night felt like a profound moral violation: she had taken something from him that he had not consented to give, and in the weeks afterward he began to see the same casual disregard for boundaries everywhere—people cutting in line, coworkers taking credit, strangers shouting at service workers—and each small transgression seemed to confirm that the world was a place where people simply took what they wanted. The humiliation was the worst part. He would replay the moment he had said yes because he was too scared to say no, and he would think: somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. Somebody smarter, somebody stronger. He came to believe that he used to be a happy person, but that version of himself was gone, replaced by someone who felt permanently marked, permanently less than.

In the months that followed, Amir found himself reacting to things he had never noticed before. When a woman on the train wore jasmine perfume, his throat would close and he would have to get off at the next stop. When a colleague said "you know what I mean" in exactly the intonation his ex had used, Amir would feel a flash of heat and a need to be somewhere else. These triggers pushed him into habits that felt necessary for survival. He began to wear concealing clothing—oversized jackets and hoodies even in warm weather—hoping to make himself invisible, to avoid being seen or noticed or evaluated. He started every day by checking the layout of whatever building he was in, locating the exits before he could focus on anything else. He avoided performance reviews and one-on-one meetings with his manager, volunteering for audit tasks that kept him in the back office rather than in client-facing roles. But each avoidance came with its own cost: when he chose the hoodie, when he declined a meeting, when he sat with his back to the wall at lunch, he told himself that this was proof of what he had become. The strategies confirmed the very appraisals that had driven him to adopt them—a loop that tightened with every repetition.

His body was never at rest. Amir felt constantly tense, his shoulders locked, his jaw clenched, his hands ready to grip something. When a coworker reached across his desk without warning, he would flinch and feel his heart hammer before his mind had registered the movement. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely—new client sites, restaurants he had not been to before—because he could not assess the danger in advance, could not know where the exits were or who might be watching him. The threat itself sharpened the triggers: the more vigilant he was, the more he noticed the smells, the more he caught people misbehaving, the more his ears snatched at phrases that echoed her voice. And his strategies kept him in a constant state of hyperawareness. By always scanning for exits, by always positioning himself defensively, by always monitoring his own visibility, he was priming his nervous system to expect danger at every turn.

By the time he sought help, Amir was twenty-two and had been living this way for nearly two years. He had stopped seeing the few friends he had kept, because every social situation required a level of evaluation he could not tolerate. His work had narrowed to the same few audit files he could complete without going to new places. What finally brought him to a therapist was a moment in the office hallway when a senior auditor brushed past him and said "oops, sorry" with a laugh that was not quite the same but close enough. He had felt the smell of jasmine from nowhere—probably just someone's hand cream—and he had stood frozen in the corridor, unable to step forward or back. When he finally made it to the bathroom, he looked at himself in the mirror, wearing the same jacket he had worn for months, and he thought: I cannot keep doing this. He wanted to feel like himself again, but he was not sure that person still existed, or whether there was anything left to find.
